Newly metamorphosed froglets of the Siberian wood frog emerge from the aquatic environment at a remarkably diminutive size, with a body mass of only 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. This neonatal wet weight is comparable to that of small-bodied bufonids and reflects the limited yolk reserves available for embryonic development before the onset of exogenous feeding. As these juveniles recruit into the terrestrial population, they undergo a prolonged period of somatic growth that ultimately culminates in the attainment of an adult body plan. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 17 °C [T = 17 °C], individuals require approximately one year to reach puberty, a developmental milestone that occurs 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth]. This extended juvenile interval is typical for temperate ranid frogs that experience a short active season and must accumulate sufficient energy reserves before investing in gametogenesis. During this pre-reproductive phase, the growing juveniles exhibit a steady allometric increase in both snout-vent length and body mass, gradually approaching the dimensions characteristic of the mature population.

Considerable sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size is evident upon the completion of growth in Rana amurensis. The maximum snout-vent length attained by adult females reaches 6.77 centimeters [Li = 6.77 centimeters], a value that significantly exceeds the corresponding measurement of 6.06 centimeters [Li = 6.06 centimeters] recorded for conspecific males. This pattern of female-biased size dimorphism is common among ranid frogs and is often attributed to fecundity selection, wherein larger females can accommodate a greater volume of eggs within the body cavity prior to oviposition. The ultimate wet weight of a gravid female can reach up to 75 grams [Wwi = up to 75 grams], which is substantially heavier than the maximum body mass observed in reproductively active males. Such divergence in terminal body mass underscores the differential energetic allocation between the sexes during adulthood, as females must channel substantial resources into the production of large gelatinous egg masses each breeding season.

The onset of reproductive capability is marked by a distinct inflection point in the growth trajectory of both sexes. Females of the Siberian wood frog generally attain sexual maturity when their snout-vent length reaches approximately 3.95 centimeters [Lp = approximately 3.95 centimeters], at which point the body mass is estimated to be around 14.9 grams [Wwp = around 14.9 grams]. Males, in contrast, tend to mature at a slightly larger body length of 4.25 centimeters [Lp = 4.25 centimeters], a difference that may relate to the acoustic and social demands of male-male competition for access to females during the breeding chorus. The attainment of these size thresholds signals the completion of the juvenile growth phase and the physiological readiness of the gonads to initiate gametogenesis. Once mature, individuals channel a considerable proportion of their acquired energy into reproductive tissues, and the disparity between the size at puberty and the ultimate adult length indicates a substantial scope for post-maturational growth, particularly in females that continue to increase in size throughout their reproductive lifespan.

Reproductive output in Rana amurensis is characterized by considerable plasticity, with individual females depositing clutches that range from 250 to 4000 eggs in one or two clutches per year [Ri = 250 to 4000 eggs in one or two clutches per year] when environmental conditions are favorable. Under the thermal regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], this annual output reflects the species' ability to exploit ephemeral water bodies across its extensive Siberian range, where the length of the hydroperiod can vary dramatically from year to year. The capacity to partition the annual reproductive investment into multiple clutches provides a bet-hedging advantage against unpredictable pond desiccation events, which can lead to total brood loss if all eggs are deposited at a single site. While the total annual fecundity is high, the actual number of surviving offspring that successfully undergo the larval-juvenile transition is strongly modulated by density-dependent factors within the aquatic tadpole community, including competition for algal food resources and the presence of invertebrate predators.

Longevity data collected from field-marked populations indicate that the maximum lifespan of the Siberian wood frog is approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] in individuals maintained under near-natural conditions at a constant 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan for a small-bodied anuran is consistent with the species' adaptation to a harsh, seasonal environment where reproductive opportunities may be limited by the brief summer window. Across this period, adult females experience a gradual decline in both body condition and clutch viability with advancing age, although senescence rates appear to be comparatively slow in this lineage. The interplay between the protracted time to maturity and the extended adult lifespan suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes iteroparity over a single, explosive breeding effort. This contrasts with the boom-and-bust tactics observed in more short-lived, arid-adapted ranids, highlighting how the cold, stable thermal environment of the Siberian taiga has shaped the demographic parameters of this hardy species.
